argument: Building on later Heidegger's question of whether we can think without the will, the episode uses Simon Critchley's book On Mysticism to present mysticism as a gateway out of the subject/object framing and toward releasement or letting-be. It clears up the misconception that mystics were irrational: the word 'mystic' was coined around the 1700s in a climate hostile to religion, and figures like Teresa of Avila, the Kabbalists, and Sufi practitioners reached their experiences through highly structured, rational devotional practice. The validity of such experiences lies not in pointing to a material cause but in subjective transformation, and having a concept of the divine available in how you frame the world greatly increases your chances of having one. Modern adulthood's self-obsession makes this hard, yet since the Protestant Reformation these experiences have been democratized through art, music, and especially poetry, which gets closer than ordinary subject-acting-on-object language ever can.
keyIdeas: Heidegger's later work moves from freedom of the will to freedom from the will, exploring releasement or letting-be as an alternative to willing ourselves onto a world of objects.

The word 'mystic' was created around the 1700s in a cultural climate hostile to religious approaches, and most people we now call mystics never used the label or opposed reason; they reached their experiences through highly rational, structured devotional practice.

Using Bernard McGinn's description, mystical experiences fall into two categories: the self transcending toward unity with something greater, or the self dissolving and being pushed aside to make room for it.

Against the skeptic demanding a material cause for the divine, the validity of these experiences lies at the level of subjective transformation, making the better question whether a devotional practice can reliably lead people to them.

Modern life blocks these experiences, since we instantly rationalize overwhelming moments and live what Critchley calls the abdication of ecstasy, but since the Protestant Reformation they have been democratized through artwork, music, deep reading, and poetry.

terms.def: Later Heidegger's name for a freedom from the will, a way of relating to being that moves beyond constantly willing ourselves onto a world of objects.
A label coined around the 1700s in a climate hostile to religious approaches, applied retroactively to people who rarely called themselves that and were not opposed to reason.
Following Bernard McGinn, an experience where the self either transcends toward unity with something greater or dissolves to make room for it, often feeling more real than reality.
The approach that studies subjective experience as worthy in its own right, rather than asking how mental events correspond to some material cause.
Critchley's phrase for modern adulthood, where constant self-obsession and busyness make the self-forgetting, ecstatic side of life nearly impossible to access.

anchors: Releasement or letting-be to Heidegger… is going to involve us going from the standard subject/object framing of things…freedom OF the will in the Nietzschean sense…to freedom FROM the will
MYSTIC is a word that was actually created fairly RECENTLY, AROUND the 1700’s…and it was created in a VERY specific cultural climate that was hostile TOWARDS the more religious approach
this is NOT the picture of someone HOSTILE towards rationality…this is the picture of someone HIGHLY COMMITTED to a devotional practice that they gave EVERYTHING they HAD to

One is where someone transcends the self…and experiences a feeling of unity or communion with the divine or something greater than themselves. The other is in the opposite direction: where the self dissolves or is pushed aside
the VALIDITY of this type of experience comes down NOT to whether it connects to some CAUSE in the material world. The REALITY of this goes ON at the level of subjective transformation.
JUST having the CONCEPT AVAILABLE to you in the way that you frame things…seems to HIGHLY increase your CHANCES…of HAVING one of these mystical experiences
We INSTANTLY start trying to rationally subordinate the moment and the feelings going on…and turn them into things we can understand, manipulate and optimize for efficiency.

adulthood is what he calls the abdication of ecstasy…we live SO much of our LIVES as adults obsessing over ourselves and our own egos…that it makes it next to IMPOSSIBLE for us to experience this entire other side of what life can be.
he says something HAPPENED, notably after the Protestant Reformation in the western world…where these experiences became sort of democratized in a way that had never really been available before.
because so often poetry is written FROM a human, subjective point of view. The HUMAN experience is often PRESUPPOSED when you’re reading a poem.

it’s ultimately a category error: we’re trying to describe something in the ontological realm PURELY with words and rational constrictions that only make sense in the realm of the ontic, subjects and objects.
there are MANY different TYPES of mysticism, that APPROACH these experiences from different premises than this one. SOME types of mysticism… will even STEER INTO the self as a starting point.
it’s like okay… if I believe in a leprechaun its way easier to believe there’s a pot o gold at the end of a rainbow. But what does that have ANYTHING to do with MY reality?
you didn’t have a CELLPHONE to turn to. You just sacrificed a big piece of yourself… OVER to this near CONSTANT process of religious contemplation.
one thing Critchley might recommend is to NOT see this as a zero sum game.
there’s no such thing as an atheist when you’re listening to music you love.
if you’re TRULY working to surrender yourself OVER to the process of internalizing these ideas, particularly the type of philosophy that tries to challenge the limits of human thought

this change often goes down most of the time in small increments, over the course of months or years, with little openings going on, prying you more and more in the direction of seeing things without so many filters on all the time.
Mysticism is a tendency more than ANYTHING to Simon Critchley.
COULD this more MEANINGFUL connection with the world… be something that we’re sadly MISSING in the modern world
